title: Organic Chemistry Foundations
description: Bonding and hybridization in carbon compounds, functional groups, naming basics, isomers, physical properties, and simple reactions: combustion, addition, substitution, elimination, oxidation and esterification.

cards.title: Which functional group is in $\ce{CH3CO2CH2CH3}$?
cards.body:
Ester ($\mathrm{RCO_2R'}$)

An **ester** has a carbonyl carbon bonded to an $\ce{O-R}$ group.

Watch out: don't confuse it with a carboxylic acid $\mathrm{RCO_2H}$ (O–H instead of O–R), an ether $\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$ (no C=O), a ketone $\mathrm{RCOR'}$, an aldehyde $\mathrm{RCHO}$, or an amide $\mathrm{RCONR_2}$ (N on the carbonyl carbon; an amine has no C=O).
cards.searchQuery: ester functional group ethyl ethanoate identify

cards.title: How many degrees of unsaturation does $\ce{C5H5N}$ have?
cards.body:
4

$$\mathrm{DoU} = \frac{2C + 2 + N - H - X}{2} = \frac{10 + 2 + 1 - 5}{2} = 4$$

Each ring or $\pi$ bond counts 1, and a triple bond counts 2. Ignore oxygen. Pyridine fits: one ring plus three $\pi$ bonds.

Watch out: nitrogen adds to the numerator, while halogens $X$ subtract like hydrogen.
cards.searchQuery: degrees of unsaturation formula C5H5N pyridine

cards.title: Why is a carboxylic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 4$–$5$) so much more acidic than an alcohol ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 16$–$18$)?
cards.body:
Its conjugate base is **resonance-stabilized**.

A carboxylate's negative charge is shared equally by two O atoms, while an alkoxide's charge sits on one O.

Key idea: the more stable the conjugate base, the stronger the acid.

Example: other rough $\mathrm{p}K_a$ values are phenol $\approx 10$, terminal alkyne $\approx 25$ and alkane $\approx 50$.
cards.searchQuery: carboxylic acid more acidic than alcohol resonance carboxylate

cards.title: How many chirality centers does 3-methylhexane have?
cards.body:
1 (C3)

C3 carries four different groups: $\ce{H}$, $\ce{CH3}$, $\ce{CH2CH3}$ and $\ce{CH2CH2CH3}$. Every other carbon is a $\ce{CH2}$ or $\ce{CH3}$ with at least two identical H atoms.

Watch out: ethyl and propyl count as different groups, so don't miss C3.
cards.searchQuery: 3-methylhexane chirality center stereocenter count

cards.title: Rank these substituents by CIP priority: $\ce{-CH2OH}$, $\ce{-CH(CH3)2}$, $\ce{-CH2Br}$, $\ce{-OH}$.
cards.body:
$\ce{-OH}$ > $\ce{-CH2Br}$ > $\ce{-CH2OH}$ > $\ce{-CH(CH3)2}$

First compare the directly attached atoms: O beats C. For ties, compare the sets of atoms on the next position and stop at the first difference: $\{\ce{Br},\ce{H},\ce{H}\}$ > $\{\ce{O},\ce{H},\ce{H}\}$ > $\{\ce{C},\ce{C},\ce{H}\}$.

Watch out: compare the sets atom by atom, highest first. One heavy atom beats several lighter ones.
cards.searchQuery: CIP priority rules rank substituents atomic number

cards.title: How are (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromopentane and (2S,3R)-2,3-dibromopentane related?
cards.body:
Diastereomers

Only one of the two chirality centers differs. They are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, and they have different physical properties.

Watch out: **enantiomers** have every center inverted, for example (2R,3R) and (2S,3S), and are nonsuperimposable mirror images.
cards.searchQuery: diastereomers versus enantiomers definition one center inverted

cards.title: How many stereoisomers does 2,3-dibromobutane have?
cards.body:
3, not $2^2 = 4$

(2R,3R) and (2S,3S) are a pair of enantiomers. (2R,3S) is a **meso** compound: an internal mirror plane makes it achiral and identical to (2S,3R).

Key idea: meso compounds have chirality centers but are optically inactive.
cards.searchQuery: 2,3-dibromobutane stereoisomers meso compound count

cards.title: In an $\mathrm{S_N2}$ reaction, what happens to the configuration of the carbon that is attacked?
cards.body:
Inversion of configuration (Walden inversion)

The nucleophile attacks from the back side, $180^\circ$ from the leaving group, in one concerted step.

Example: (R)-2-bromobutane + $\ce{CN-}$ gives (S)-2-methylbutanenitrile.

Watch out: the geometry always inverts, but the label R/S flips only if the nucleophile ranks where the leaving group did.
cards.searchQuery: SN2 inversion of configuration backside attack Walden inversion

cards.title: $\mathrm{S_N2}$: what is the rate law, and how do methyl, 1°, 2° and 3° alkyl halides rank in reactivity?
cards.body:
$\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{Nu^-}]$, and methyl > 1° > 2° $\gg$ 3°.

The reaction is second order overall. Tertiary halides essentially don't react by this path.

Why: bulky groups block the backside attack (steric hindrance). Doubling either the substrate or the nucleophile concentration doubles the rate.
cards.searchQuery: SN2 rate law substrate reactivity methyl primary secondary tertiary

cards.title: Which solvent type favors $\mathrm{S_N2}$, and which favors $\mathrm{S_N1}$?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{S_N2}$: polar aprotic (DMSO, DMF, acetone, acetonitrile). $\mathrm{S_N1}$: polar protic (water, alcohols).

Aprotic solvents can't hydrogen-bond to an anionic nucleophile, leaving it "naked" and reactive.

Why: protic solvents stabilize the carbocation and the leaving group by solvation, which speeds ionization.
cards.searchQuery: polar aprotic versus polar protic solvent SN2 SN1

cards.title: What is the stereochemical outcome when (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane undergoes $\mathrm{S_N1}$ solvolysis in water?
cards.body:
Racemization

The product is a nearly 50:50 mix of R and S alcohols. The leaving group departs first (rate $= k[\mathrm{RX}]$, unimolecular), giving a planar $sp^2$ carbocation that water can attack from either face.

Watch out: there is often a slight excess of inversion, because the departing $\ce{Br-}$ briefly shields one face.
cards.searchQuery: SN1 racemization planar carbocation stereochemistry

cards.title: For E2 on a cyclohexane ring, what positions must the leaving group and the β-hydrogen occupy?
cards.body:
Both axial, on opposite faces (trans-diaxial), which makes them anti-periplanar ($180^\circ$).

E2 is concerted, so the breaking C–H and C–X bonds must line up. If the leaving group is equatorial, the ring must flip to put it axial first.

Key idea: E2 needs a strong base, and the rate is $k[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{base}]$.
cards.searchQuery: E2 elimination anti-periplanar trans-diaxial cyclohexane

cards.title: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane + potassium tert-butoxide (a bulky base): what is the major alkene product?
cards.body:
2-Methyl-1-butene, the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene

The bulky base removes the most accessible H, on a $\ce{CH3}$ group.

Watch out: a small strong base such as sodium ethoxide ($\ce{NaOEt}$) mainly gives the more substituted (**Zaitsev**) alkene, 2-methyl-2-butene.
cards.searchQuery: Hofmann versus Zaitsev bulky base potassium tert-butoxide 2-methyl-1-butene

cards.title: Propene reacts with $\ce{HBr}$ (no peroxides present). What is the major product?
cards.body:
2-Bromopropane

**Markovnikov** addition: $\ce{H+}$ adds to the $\ce{CH2}$ end (the carbon with more H atoms) to give the more stable $2^\circ$ carbocation, which $\ce{Br-}$ then attacks.

Watch out: with peroxides ($\ce{ROOR}$), $\ce{HBr}$ adds by a radical path in an anti-Markovnikov way, giving 1-bromopropane.
cards.searchQuery: Markovnikov rule propene HBr 2-bromopropane

cards.title: $\ce{HBr}$ adds to 3-methyl-1-butene. What is the major product?
cards.body:
2-Bromo-2-methylbutane

Protonation gives a $2^\circ$ carbocation. A 1,2-hydride shift from the neighboring CH makes a more stable $3^\circ$ carbocation, which $\ce{Br-}$ traps.

Why: carbocation stability is $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ >$ methyl, from hyperconjugation and induction.
Watch out: the unrearranged product, 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, is minor.
cards.searchQuery: carbocation rearrangement hydride shift 3-methyl-1-butene HBr

cards.title: Propene is treated with (1) $\ce{BH3}\cdot$THF, then (2) $\ce{H2O2}$, $\ce{NaOH}$. What is the major product?
cards.body:
1-Propanol (anti-Markovnikov OH)

Boron adds to the less substituted carbon and H to the more substituted one in a concerted **syn addition**, so no carbocation forms and nothing rearranges. Oxidation then swaps B for OH with retention.

Watch out: acid-catalyzed hydration instead gives 2-propanol.
cards.searchQuery: hydroboration oxidation propene 1-propanol anti-Markovnikov syn addition

cards.title: How many covalent bonds does a neutral carbon atom almost always form in organic compounds?
cards.body:
4

Carbon has four valence electrons, so it shares them to complete an octet with four bonds. They can be single, double or triple bonds, as long as the total is four.

Example: methane $\ce{CH4}$ has four single bonds, ethene $\ce{CH2=CH2}$ has two C–H bonds and one double bond on each carbon, and ethyne $\ce{HC#CH}$ has one C–H and one triple bond on each carbon.

Key idea: when you count bonds in a structure, **every carbon needs four**.
cards.searchQuery: carbon forms four covalent bonds organic chemistry valence

cards.title: What is the hybridization of carbon in methane, and what is the H–C–H bond angle?
cards.body:
$sp^3$, with bond angles of about $109.5^\circ$ (tetrahedral).

One $s$ and three $p$ orbitals mix to form four equivalent $sp^3$ hybrid orbitals, which point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

Key idea: four electron groups around a carbon mean **tetrahedral**, $sp^3$ and $109.5^\circ$.
cards.searchQuery: methane sp3 hybridization tetrahedral 109.5 degrees

cards.title: What is the hybridization of each carbon in ethene ($\ce{CH2=CH2}$), and what is the approximate H–C–H angle?
cards.body:
$sp^2$, about $120^\circ$ (trigonal planar).

Each carbon uses three $sp^2$ orbitals for its three $\sigma$ bonds. The leftover $p$ orbital overlaps sideways with its neighbor's to form the $\pi$ bond.

Key idea: all six atoms of ethene lie in **one plane**.
cards.searchQuery: ethene sp2 hybridization trigonal planar 120 degrees pi bond

cards.title: What is the hybridization of each carbon in ethyne, $\ce{HC#CH}$?
cards.body:
$sp$

Each carbon mixes one $s$ and one $p$ orbital and has two $\pi$ bonds from its two leftover $p$ orbitals. The $\ce{H-C#C-H}$ unit is linear, with $180^\circ$ bond angles.

Key idea: triple bond means $sp$ and linear; double bond means $sp^2$ and planar; single bonds only means $sp^3$.
cards.searchQuery: ethyne sp hybridization linear triple bond

cards.title: How many $\sigma$ bonds and how many $\pi$ bonds are in ethene, $\ce{CH2=CH2}$?
cards.body:
5 $\sigma$ bonds and 1 $\pi$ bond.

There are four C–H $\sigma$ bonds and one C–C $\sigma$ bond. The second bond of the double bond is the single $\pi$ bond.

Tip: a double bond is one $\sigma$ plus one $\pi$; a triple bond is one $\sigma$ plus two $\pi$.
cards.searchQuery: ethene number of sigma and pi bonds double bond

cards.title: Rank the carbon–carbon bonds $\ce{C-C}$, $\ce{C=C}$ and $\ce{C#C}$ from longest to shortest.
cards.body:
$\ce{C-C}$ > $\ce{C=C}$ > $\ce{C#C}$

Typical lengths are about $154\,\mathrm{pm}$, $134\,\mathrm{pm}$ and $120\,\mathrm{pm}$. More shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer.

Key idea: more bonds between two atoms means a **shorter and stronger** bond.
cards.searchQuery: carbon carbon bond length single double triple comparison

cards.title: What is the general molecular formula of an acyclic alkane with $n$ carbon atoms?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}$

A saturated chain carries two H atoms on each carbon, plus one extra H on each end.

Example: for $n = 3$ this gives $\ce{C3H8}$, propane.

Watch out: a ring or a double bond removes two H atoms, so those compounds have fewer than $2n+2$ H atoms.
cards.searchQuery: alkane general formula CnH2n+2 saturated hydrocarbon

cards.title: What is the general molecular formula of a cycloalkane with one ring and $n$ carbon atoms?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$

Forming the ring removes two H atoms compared with the open-chain alkane $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}$, so it has one degree of unsaturation.

Example: cyclohexane is $\ce{C6H12}$.

Watch out: a one-ring cycloalkane has the same formula as an alkene with the same number of carbons.
cards.searchQuery: cycloalkane general formula CnH2n ring degree of unsaturation

cards.title: In a skeletal (line-angle) structure, what do the line ends and bends represent, and where are the hydrogen atoms on carbon?
cards.body:
Each end and each bend is a carbon atom; the H atoms bonded to carbon are not drawn.

You add enough implied H atoms to give each carbon four bonds. Atoms other than C and H are written out, and so are the H atoms attached to them (as in $\ce{OH}$).

Example: a zigzag line with four carbons (two ends and two bends) is butane, $\ce{C4H10}$.

Watch out: a line ending in $\ce{OH}$ shows an alcohol, and its carbon end still counts as a carbon.
cards.searchQuery: skeletal structure line-angle formula implied carbons hydrogens

cards.title: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2OH}$?
cards.body:
12

Add them group by group: $\ce{CH3}$ (3), $\ce{CH2}$ (2), $\ce{CH}$ (1), $\ce{CH3}$ (3), $\ce{CH2}$ (2) and $\ce{OH}$ (1), which gives 12. The molecular formula is $\ce{C5H12O}$.

Tip: check your count against the degrees of unsaturation. With no rings or $\pi$ bonds, $\ce{C5H12O}$ is saturated ($2 \times 5 + 2 = 12$ H atoms).
cards.searchQuery: condensed structural formula count hydrogens C5H12O

cards.title: What are the IUPAC root names for unbranched chains of 1 to 10 carbons?
cards.body:
meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-, non-, dec-

Add **-ane** for an alkane: methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane, hexane, heptane, octane, nonane, decane.

Mnemonic: "Monkeys Eat Peeled Bananas" for the first four (meth, eth, prop, but).
cards.searchQuery: IUPAC alkane names C1 to C10 methane to decane prefixes

cards.title: What is the name of the unbranched alkane with 8 carbon atoms?
cards.body:
Octane

The root **oct-** means eight, and the suffix **-ane** shows that all the carbon–carbon bonds are single.

Example: octane is $\ce{C8H18}$, which fits $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}$ with $n = 8$.
cards.searchQuery: octane eight carbon alkane name C8H18

cards.title: In IUPAC naming of an alkane, how do you choose the parent chain?
cards.body:
Choose the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms.

The chain may bend around the drawing. Everything not in the chain is named as a substituent.

Watch out: if two chains tie in length, pick the one with **more substituents**.

Tip: draw the structure out in full before you decide, because the longest chain is often not the one written in a straight line.
cards.searchQuery: IUPAC naming alkanes longest continuous chain parent chain rule

cards.title: In IUPAC naming of a branched alkane, how do you number the parent chain?
cards.body:
Number from the end that gives the first substituent the lowest number.

If the two directions tie at the first substituent, go to the next point of difference. Substituents are listed in alphabetical order, ignoring prefixes such as di- and tri-.

Example: $\ce{CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3}$ is 2-methylbutane, not 3-methylbutane.

Watch out: always compare the whole set of numbers, not just the largest one.
cards.searchQuery: IUPAC numbering rule lowest locants substituents alkane

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3}$?
cards.body:
2-Methylbutane

The longest chain has four carbons (butane), with a methyl group on the second carbon from either end.

Tip: its common name is **isopentane**; it is an isomer of pentane, $\ce{C5H12}$, with one methyl branch near the end.
cards.searchQuery: 2-methylbutane isopentane structure IUPAC name

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of $\ce{C(CH3)4}$?
cards.body:
2,2-Dimethylpropane

The longest chain has three carbons (propane), and two methyl groups are on the central carbon, so the locants are 2,2. The common name is **neopentane**.

Watch out: the number is repeated for each identical group: 2,2-dimethyl, not 2-dimethyl.
cards.searchQuery: 2,2-dimethylpropane neopentane name structure

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH2CH3)CH2CH2CH3}$?
cards.body:
3-Ethylhexane

The longest chain runs through the branching carbon and has six carbons, using the propyl arm and one ethyl arm. The other ethyl group is the substituent, on C3.

Watch out: it is not 3-propylpentane, which would use a shorter parent chain.
cards.searchQuery: 3-ethylhexane IUPAC naming longest chain branched alkane

cards.title: What is the common name of the alkyl group $\ce{-CH(CH3)2}$?
cards.body:
Isopropyl

It is a propyl group attached through its middle carbon, so the carbon that bonds to the rest of the molecule also carries two methyl groups. Its IUPAC-style name is propan-2-yl.

Example: 2-bromopropane can be called isopropyl bromide.
cards.searchQuery: isopropyl group CH(CH3)2 alkyl group name

cards.title: What is the common name of the alkyl group $\ce{-C(CH3)3}$?
cards.body:
tert-Butyl

The carbon that attaches to the molecule is bonded to three other carbons (a tertiary carbon).

Example: **tert-butyl** is the bulky group in tert-butanol and in potassium tert-butoxide.

Watch out: butyl, isobutyl, sec-butyl and tert-butyl are four different $\ce{C4H9}$ groups.
cards.searchQuery: tert-butyl group C(CH3)3 alkyl group name

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of the compound formed when one H atom of cyclohexane is replaced by $\ce{CH3}$?
cards.body:
Methylcyclohexane

With a single substituent on a ring, no number is needed, because every ring position is equivalent. The ring is the parent when it has more carbons than the substituent.

Tip: with two or more substituents, number the ring so that they get the lowest possible numbers, starting at a substituted carbon.
cards.searchQuery: methylcyclohexane naming substituted cycloalkanes

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3}$ (ignoring cis/trans)?
cards.body:
But-2-ene (2-butene)

The four-carbon chain gives **but-**, the double bond gives **-ene**, and the 2 shows that the double bond starts at carbon 2.

Watch out: $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH3}$ is a different compound, but-1-ene.
cards.searchQuery: but-2-ene 2-butene naming alkenes double bond position

cards.title: What suffix in IUPAC names marks a carbon–carbon triple bond?
cards.body:
-yne

The position is given by a number, as for alkenes, and the chain is numbered to give the triple bond the lowest number.

Example: $\ce{HC#C-CH2CH3}$ is but-1-yne and $\ce{CH3C#CCH3}$ is but-2-yne.

Tip: **-ane** is all single bonds, **-ene** has a double bond and **-yne** has a triple bond.
cards.searchQuery: alkyne suffix yne naming triple bond IUPAC

cards.title: When naming an alkene, which comes first in numbering the chain: the double bond or a substituent?
cards.body:
The double bond

The parent chain must contain the $\ce{C=C}$, and you number it so that the double bond gets the lowest possible number. Substituent numbers come second.

Example: $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH(CH3)CH3}$ is 4-methylpent-2-ene, not 2-methylpent-3-ene.

Watch out: the parent chain is the longest chain containing the double bond, which is not always the longest chain overall.
cards.searchQuery: naming alkenes numbering double bond lowest number priority substituents

cards.title: What is the name of the $\ce{C=O}$ functional group found in aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and amides?
cards.body:
Carbonyl

The carbon is $sp^2$ and trigonal planar. The $\ce{C=O}$ bond is polar, with a partial positive charge on carbon, so carbonyl carbons are attacked by nucleophiles.

Key idea: what the carbonyl carbon is bonded to decides the family: H or C gives an aldehyde or ketone, O gives an acid or ester, and N gives an amide.
cards.searchQuery: carbonyl group C=O functional group aldehydes ketones acids

cards.title: Which class of organic compound has an $\ce{-OH}$ group bonded to a saturated ($sp^3$) carbon?
cards.body:
Alcohol

The IUPAC suffix is **-ol**, as in ethanol, $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$.

Watch out: if the $\ce{-OH}$ is attached directly to a benzene ring, the compound is a phenol, not an alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: alcohol functional group hydroxyl sp3 carbon suffix -ol

cards.title: Which functional group is $\mathrm{R{-}CHO}$, a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one hydrogen, found at the end of a carbon chain?
cards.body:
Aldehyde

The IUPAC suffix is **-al**, as in ethanal, $\ce{CH3CHO}$. The aldehyde carbon is always carbon 1 of the chain.

Watch out: an aldehyde has an H on the carbonyl carbon; a ketone has two carbon groups there.
cards.searchQuery: aldehyde functional group RCHO suffix -al carbonyl at chain end

cards.title: Which functional group is $\mathrm{R{-}CO{-}R'}$, a carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbon groups?
cards.body:
Ketone

The IUPAC suffix is **-one**, as in propanone, $\ce{CH3COCH3}$. The carbonyl is never at the end of the chain, so the name needs a position number from pentanone onward.

Watch out: both groups on the carbonyl carbon must be carbons; if one is O it is an ester or acid, and if one is N it is an amide.
cards.searchQuery: ketone functional group RCOR carbonyl two carbons suffix -one

cards.title: Which functional group is $\ce{-COOH}$, a carbonyl carbon bonded to an $\ce{-OH}$ group?
cards.body:
Carboxylic acid

The IUPAC suffix is **-oic acid**, as in ethanoic acid, $\ce{CH3COOH}$. The acidic H is the one on oxygen.

Example: carboxylic acids are weak acids, with $\mathrm{p}K_a$ about $4$–$5$, but much stronger than alcohols.
cards.searchQuery: carboxylic acid functional group COOH suffix -oic acid

cards.title: Which class of organic compound contains a nitrogen atom bonded to carbon with no carbonyl group, such as $\ce{CH3CH2NH2}$?
cards.body:
Amine

The nitrogen has a lone pair, so amines are weak bases and nucleophiles. The IUPAC suffix is **-amine**, as in ethanamine.

Watch out: if the nitrogen is bonded to a carbonyl carbon, the compound is an amide, which is not basic.
cards.searchQuery: amine functional group nitrogen lone pair weak base

cards.title: Which functional group is $\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$, an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon groups?
cards.body:
Ether

Ethers have no O–H bond, so they cannot hydrogen-bond to each other. They boil far lower than alcohols of similar mass.

Example: diethyl ether, $\ce{CH3CH2OCH2CH3}$, is a common solvent.

Watch out: ethers lack a carbonyl group. If there is a $\ce{C=O}$ next to the oxygen, it is an ester.
cards.searchQuery: ether functional group R-O-R diethyl ether properties

cards.title: What class of organic compound is $\ce{CH3CH2Br}$?
cards.body:
Alkyl halide (haloalkane)

It contains a carbon–halogen bond ($\ce{C-F}$, $\ce{C-Cl}$, $\ce{C-Br}$ or $\ce{C-I}$). It is named as a substituted alkane: $\ce{CH3CH2Br}$ is bromoethane.

Why: the carbon–halogen bond is polar, so the carbon is electrophilic and alkyl halides react with nucleophiles.
cards.searchQuery: alkyl halide haloalkane functional group bromoethane

cards.title: What is the name of the functional group $\ce{-C#N}$?
cards.body:
Nitrile (cyano group)

The nitrile carbon is counted in the main chain, and the suffix is **-nitrile**. The carbon and nitrogen are both $sp$ hybridized, so $\ce{C-C#N}$ is linear.

Example: $\ce{CH3CN}$ is ethanenitrile (acetonitrile), a common polar aprotic solvent.
cards.searchQuery: nitrile functional group cyano C#N naming

cards.title: What is the name of the planar six-carbon ring of formula $\ce{C6H6}$ whose $\pi$ electrons are delocalized around the ring?
cards.body:
Benzene

All six C–C bonds are the same length ($140\,\mathrm{pm}$), between a single and a double bond, and every carbon is $sp^2$. The delocalized ring is unusually stable, which is called **aromaticity**.

Watch out: benzene is not three separate double bonds that flip back and forth. The two Kekulé drawings are resonance forms of one structure.
cards.searchQuery: benzene C6H6 aromatic ring delocalized pi electrons stability

cards.title: What is the compound class when an $\ce{-OH}$ group is bonded directly to a benzene ring?
cards.body:
Phenol

The simplest phenol is $\ce{C6H5OH}$, also called phenol. It is more acidic than an ordinary alcohol ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 10$), because the phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance with the ring.

Watch out: phenols are still much weaker acids than carboxylic acids.
cards.searchQuery: phenol functional group OH benzene ring acidity

cards.title: How is an alcohol classified as primary, secondary or tertiary?
cards.body:
By the number of carbon groups attached to the carbon that bears the $\ce{-OH}$: one for primary ($1^\circ$), two for secondary ($2^\circ$) and three for tertiary ($3^\circ$).

Example: ethanol is $1^\circ$, 2-propanol is $2^\circ$ and 2-methyl-2-propanol is $3^\circ$.

Why: the class decides what happens on oxidation, since a $1^\circ$ alcohol gives an aldehyde or acid, a $2^\circ$ alcohol gives a ketone, and a $3^\circ$ alcohol resists oxidation.
cards.searchQuery: primary secondary tertiary alcohol classification carbon bearing OH

cards.title: How is an amine classified as primary, secondary or tertiary?
cards.body:
By the number of carbon groups attached to the nitrogen: one for primary, two for secondary and three for tertiary.

Example: $\ce{CH3NH2}$ is primary, $\ce{(CH3)2NH}$ is secondary and $\ce{(CH3)3N}$ is tertiary.

Watch out: this differs from alcohols and alkyl halides, which are classed by the carbon bearing the group. tert-Butylamine, $\ce{(CH3)3CNH2}$, is a **primary** amine.
cards.searchQuery: primary secondary tertiary amine classification nitrogen carbon groups

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3COCH3}$?
cards.body:
Propanone (also called acetone)

The three-carbon chain gives **prop-** and the ketone suffix gives **-one**. No number is needed, because the carbonyl can only be on the middle carbon.

Example: propanone is a common solvent, for instance in nail polish remover.
cards.searchQuery: propanone acetone IUPAC name simplest ketone

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3CHO}$?
cards.body:
Ethanal (also called acetaldehyde)

The two-carbon chain gives **eth-**, and the aldehyde suffix is **-al**. The aldehyde carbon is carbon 1.

Example: ethanal forms when ethanol is oxidized, and it is an intermediate in alcohol metabolism.
cards.searchQuery: ethanal acetaldehyde CH3CHO IUPAC name aldehyde

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3COOH}$?
cards.body:
Ethanoic acid (also called acetic acid)

The two-carbon chain gives **eth-** and the acid suffix is **-oic acid**. The carboxyl carbon is carbon 1 and is counted in the chain.

Example: vinegar is about 5% ethanoic acid in water.
cards.searchQuery: ethanoic acid acetic acid CH3COOH IUPAC name vinegar

cards.title: What is the IUPAC name of the ester $\ce{CH3COOCH2CH3}$?
cards.body:
Ethyl ethanoate (also called ethyl acetate)

Name the alkyl group on oxygen first (ethyl), then the acid part with the ending **-oate** (ethanoate). The acid part is the side that contains the carbonyl.

Watch out: methyl propanoate, $\ce{CH3CH2COOCH3}$, is an isomer, so the order of the two parts matters.
cards.searchQuery: ethyl ethanoate ethyl acetate ester naming alkyl alkanoate

cards.title: How does the boiling point of unbranched alkanes change as the chain gets longer, and why?
cards.body:
It rises, because longer chains have stronger London dispersion forces.

More electrons and a larger surface area allow stronger temporary induced dipoles between neighboring molecules.

Example: pentane boils at $36\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and hexane at $69\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Key idea: alkanes are nonpolar, so **dispersion forces** are their only intermolecular force.
cards.searchQuery: alkane boiling point trend chain length London dispersion forces

cards.title: Pentane boils at $36\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ but its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane boils at $9.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Why?
cards.body:
Branching makes the molecule more compact, so there is less surface contact and weaker dispersion forces.

Straight chains lie alongside each other and touch along their whole length. A compact, nearly spherical molecule touches its neighbors at only a few points.

Key idea: for isomers, **more branching** means a lower boiling point.
cards.searchQuery: branching lowers boiling point isomers pentane neopentane surface area

cards.title: What term describes compounds with the same molecular formula but different connectivity of their atoms?
cards.body:
Constitutional isomers (structural isomers)

Their atoms are bonded in a different order, so they are different compounds with different properties.

Example: butane and 2-methylpropane are both $\ce{C4H10}$, but one is a straight chain and the other is branched.

Watch out: stereoisomers have the same connectivity and differ only in 3D arrangement.
cards.searchQuery: constitutional isomers definition same molecular formula different connectivity

cards.title: How many constitutional isomers have the molecular formula $\ce{C4H10}$?
cards.body:
2

They are butane (an unbranched chain) and 2-methylpropane (isobutane), which has a branch.

Tip: to count isomers, work from the longest chain down, shortening it by one carbon and moving the branches to every distinct position.
cards.searchQuery: butane isomers C4H10 butane and isobutane constitutional

cards.title: How many constitutional isomers have the molecular formula $\ce{C5H12}$?
cards.body:
3

They are pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

Watch out: 3-methylbutane is not a separate isomer; numbered from the other end it is 2-methylbutane.
cards.searchQuery: pentane isomers C5H12 three constitutional isomers

cards.title: How many constitutional isomers have the molecular formula $\ce{C6H14}$?
cards.body:
5

They are hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane.

Watch out: always check that two drawings are not the same molecule, for example 2-methylpentane written backwards.
cards.searchQuery: hexane isomers C6H14 five constitutional isomers

cards.title: How many constitutional isomers have the molecular formula $\ce{C3H8O}$?
cards.body:
3

Two are alcohols, 1-propanol and 2-propanol, and one is an ether, methoxyethane ($\ce{CH3OCH2CH3}$).

Key idea: when the formula has oxygen, consider **both** alcohols and ethers.
cards.searchQuery: C3H8O isomers propanol isopropanol methoxyethane count

cards.title: Ethanol and dimethyl ether both have the formula $\ce{C2H6O}$. What kind of isomers are they?
cards.body:
Functional group isomers, a type of constitutional isomer

They have different functional groups: ethanol is an alcohol, $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$, and dimethyl ether is an ether, $\ce{CH3OCH3}$.

Example: ethanol is a liquid at room temperature ($78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ boiling point), while dimethyl ether is a gas ($-24\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).
cards.searchQuery: functional group isomers ethanol dimethyl ether C2H6O

cards.title: Why can but-2-ene exist as cis and trans isomers, while but-1-ene cannot?
cards.body:
Each carbon of the $\ce{C=C}$ in but-2-ene carries two different groups, and rotation about a double bond is blocked.

The $\pi$ bond would have to break for the ends to rotate. In but-1-ene, one carbon of the double bond has two identical H atoms, so swapping gives the same molecule.

Key idea: **cis** means the two $\ce{CH3}$ groups are on the same side of the double bond; **trans** means opposite sides.
cards.searchQuery: cis trans isomers but-2-ene restricted rotation double bond

cards.title: What term describes a pair of stereoisomers that are nonsuperimposable mirror images of each other?
cards.body:
Enantiomers

They have the same melting point, boiling point and other physical properties (except that they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions), and react identically with achiral reagents.

Watch out: enantiomers differ at **every** chirality center. If only some centers differ, the stereoisomers are diastereomers.
cards.searchQuery: enantiomers definition nonsuperimposable mirror images stereoisomers

cards.title: What term describes a molecule that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image?
cards.body:
Chiral

The usual cause is a carbon bonded to four different groups, a chirality center. The word comes from the Greek for "hand".

Example: 2-butanol is chiral; 2-propanol is not, because the central carbon has two identical $\ce{CH3}$ groups.
cards.searchQuery: chiral molecule definition nonsuperimposable mirror image four different groups

cards.title: Ethanol boils at $78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ but propane, of similar molar mass, boils at $-42\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Which intermolecular force explains the difference?
cards.body:
Hydrogen bonding

The $\ce{O-H}$ bond of one ethanol molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of another. Propane has only weak dispersion forces.

Key idea: a molecule needs an H bonded to **N, O or F** to hydrogen-bond with its neighbors.
cards.searchQuery: ethanol hydrogen bonding boiling point compared with propane

cards.title: Why does propanone ($56\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) boil higher than butane ($-1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) but lower than 1-propanol ($97\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$)?
cards.body:
Propanone has dipole–dipole forces but no hydrogen bonding between its own molecules.

The polar $\ce{C=O}$ bond adds dipole–dipole attraction to the dispersion forces that butane has. But propanone has no O–H, so it cannot hydrogen-bond with itself, as an alcohol can.

Key idea: roughly, for similar molar mass, the boiling point order is alkane < ether < aldehyde or ketone < alcohol < carboxylic acid.
cards.searchQuery: boiling point ketone versus alkane versus alcohol dipole-dipole hydrogen bonding

cards.title: Why does ethanoic acid ($118\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) boil higher than 1-propanol ($97\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), though both have a molar mass of about $60\,\mathrm{g/mol}$?
cards.body:
Carboxylic acid molecules form hydrogen-bonded pairs (dimers) with two hydrogen bonds each.

The $\ce{C=O}$ oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor and the O–H is a donor, so each acid pairs up with another through two bonds.

Key idea: more hydrogen bonding per molecule means a **higher boiling point**.
cards.searchQuery: carboxylic acid dimer hydrogen bonding boiling point ethanoic acid

cards.title: Why does the solubility of alcohols in water decrease as the carbon chain gets longer?
cards.body:
The nonpolar hydrocarbon chain grows while the polar $\ce{-OH}$ stays the same, so the molecule becomes less like water.

Methanol, ethanol and propanol mix with water in all proportions. Larger alcohols such as 1-hexanol dissolve only slightly.

Key idea: **like dissolves like**. A long chain behaves like an alkane, which is hydrophobic.
cards.searchQuery: alcohol solubility in water decreases with chain length like dissolves like

cards.title: Complete combustion of one mole of propane, $\ce{C3H8}$, consumes how many moles of $\ce{O2}$?
cards.body:
5

$$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$$

Balance C first (3 $\ce{CO2}$), then H (4 $\ce{H2O}$), and count the oxygen last: $3 \times 2 + 4 = 10$ O atoms, so 5 $\ce{O2}$.

Tip: **balance O last**, because it appears in two products.
cards.searchQuery: propane complete combustion balanced equation oxygen moles

cards.title: Methane reacts with $\ce{Cl2}$ to form chloromethane only if what is supplied to start the reaction?
cards.body:
UV light (or strong heat)

$$\ce{CH4 + Cl2 ->[UV] CH3Cl + HCl}$$

Light splits $\ce{Cl2}$ into two chlorine radicals, and these start a radical chain reaction. In the dark at room temperature, the two do not react.

Watch out: the reaction is not selective. Further substitution gives $\ce{CH2Cl2}$, $\ce{CHCl3}$ and $\ce{CCl4}$ too, so you get a **mixture**.
cards.searchQuery: free radical chlorination methane UV light initiation

cards.title: Ethene reacts with $\ce{H2}$ over a platinum or palladium catalyst. What is the product?
cards.body:
Ethane

$$\ce{CH2=CH2 + H2 ->[Pt] CH3CH3}$$

Both H atoms add to the same face of the double bond, on the surface of the metal. The $\pi$ bond is replaced by two C–H bonds.

Key idea: hydrogenation converts an alkene into an alkane, and the alkene's formula $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$ becomes $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}$.
cards.searchQuery: alkene hydrogenation ethene to ethane platinum palladium catalyst

cards.title: What is the product when ethene reacts with $\ce{Br2}$?
cards.body:
1,2-Dibromoethane

$$\ce{CH2=CH2 + Br2 -> BrCH2CH2Br}$$

The $\pi$ bond breaks and one Br adds to each carbon, giving a vicinal dibromide (one Br on each of two adjacent carbons).

Watch out: this is an **addition** reaction. Alkanes react with $\ce{Br2}$ only by substitution, and only in light.
cards.searchQuery: ethene bromine addition 1,2-dibromoethane vicinal dibromide

cards.title: What do you observe when an alkene is shaken with bromine water (or $\ce{Br2}$ in an organic solvent)?
cards.body:
The orange-brown color of the bromine disappears.

The $\ce{Br2}$ adds across the $\ce{C=C}$ and the colorless dibromide forms. This is a simple test for **unsaturation**.

Watch out: an alkane does not decolorize bromine in the dark, so the test separates alkenes from alkanes.
cards.searchQuery: bromine water test alkene decolorizes unsaturation test

cards.title: Propene undergoes acid-catalyzed hydration ($\ce{H2O}$ with $\ce{H2SO4}$ catalyst). What is the major product?
cards.body:
2-Propanol (propan-2-ol)

After protonation, the more stable $2^\circ$ carbocation forms, and water adds there (Markovnikov addition). Loss of $\ce{H+}$ gives the alcohol.

Watch out: hydroboration–oxidation gives the other regiochemistry, 1-propanol.
cards.searchQuery: acid-catalyzed hydration propene 2-propanol Markovnikov

cards.title: What polymer forms when many ethene molecules, $\ce{CH2=CH2}$, join by addition polymerization?
cards.body:
Polyethylene (polyethene, polythene)

$$n\,\ce{CH2=CH2} \rightarrow \left(\ce{-CH2-CH2-}\right)_n$$

Each $\pi$ bond opens and the monomers link end to end into a long chain. No atoms are lost.

Example: polyethylene is used in plastic bags and bottles.
cards.searchQuery: ethene addition polymerization polyethylene monomer repeat unit

cards.title: What small molecule is lost each time two monomers join in condensation polymerization, as when a diacid and a diamine form nylon-6,6?
cards.body:
Water

Each new amide link forms by losing $\ce{H2O}$. Polyesters form the same way, from a diacid and a diol, with an ester link.

Watch out: addition polymers such as polyethylene lose nothing. Condensation polymers always release a small molecule.
cards.searchQuery: condensation polymerization water released nylon polyester amide ester link

cards.title: Ethanol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate. What organic product forms?
cards.body:
Ethanoic acid

$$\ce{CH3CH2OH ->[Cr2O7^2-/H+] CH3CHO ->[Cr2O7^2-/H+] CH3COOH}$$

A primary alcohol is oxidized first to an aldehyde and then, with excess oxidant and reflux, on to the carboxylic acid. The orange dichromate turns green as it is reduced to $\ce{Cr^3+}$.

Tip: to **stop at the aldehyde**, distil the product out as it forms or use a milder oxidant such as PCC.
cards.searchQuery: oxidation of primary alcohol ethanol to ethanoic acid acidified dichromate reflux

cards.title: Propan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. What organic product forms?
cards.body:
Propanone (acetone)

A secondary alcohol is oxidized to a ketone, and the reaction stops there because the ketone has no H on its carbonyl carbon to lose.

Example: the orange mixture turns green, showing that the alcohol has been oxidized.
cards.searchQuery: oxidation secondary alcohol propan-2-ol to propanone ketone dichromate

cards.title: Why do tertiary alcohols resist oxidation by acidified dichromate?
cards.body:
The carbon bearing the $\ce{-OH}$ has no hydrogen atom to lose.

Oxidizing an alcohol removes the H from that carbon together with the H from the OH, forming $\ce{C=O}$. A tertiary alcohol has three carbon groups there and nothing to remove, short of breaking a C–C bond.

Key idea: the dichromate stays orange with a **tertiary** alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: tertiary alcohol not oxidized no hydrogen on carbon bearing OH

cards.title: Ethanol is heated to about $170\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ with concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$. What is the main organic product?
cards.body:
Ethene

$$\ce{CH3CH2OH ->[conc. H2SO4][170 °C] CH2=CH2 + H2O}$$

The acid protonates the OH, water leaves, and a proton is lost from the neighboring carbon to form the double bond. This is an **elimination** (dehydration).

Watch out: at a lower temperature (about $140\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), two ethanol molecules combine instead and give diethyl ether.
cards.searchQuery: dehydration of ethanol concentrated sulfuric acid 170 C ethene

cards.title: Ethanoic acid is heated with ethanol and a few drops of concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$. What organic product forms?
cards.body:
Ethyl ethanoate

$$\ce{CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH <=>[H+] CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O}$$

An acid and an alcohol combine to give an ester and water. The reaction is reversible and the acid catalyst speeds it up.

Tip: to push the equilibrium toward the ester, use an excess of one reactant or remove the water.
cards.searchQuery: Fischer esterification ethanoic acid ethanol sulfuric acid ethyl ethanoate

cards.title: What are the two products when an ester is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide (saponification)?
cards.body:
A carboxylate salt and an alcohol.

$$\ce{CH3COOCH2CH3 + NaOH -> CH3COO- Na+ + CH3CH2OH}$$

The reaction goes to completion because the carboxylate ion can no longer be attacked by the alcohol.

Example: soap is made by treating a fat (a triester) with $\ce{NaOH}$, which gives glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids.
cards.searchQuery: ester base hydrolysis saponification products carboxylate salt alcohol

cards.title: Ethanoic acid reacts with aqueous $\ce{NaOH}$. What is the name of the organic salt formed?
cards.body:
Sodium ethanoate

$$\ce{CH3COOH + NaOH -> CH3COO- Na+ + H2O}$$

It is a neutralization: the acidic H of the $\ce{-COOH}$ group is removed. Carboxylate salts dissolve well in water.

Watch out: the salt is named with the acid's stem ending in **-oate**, not -oic acid.
cards.searchQuery: carboxylic acid with sodium hydroxide sodium ethanoate neutralization

cards.title: Methylamine, $\ce{CH3NH2}$, reacts with hydrochloric acid. What is the name of the product?
cards.body:
Methylammonium chloride

$$\ce{CH3NH2 + HCl -> CH3NH3+ Cl-}$$

The nitrogen lone pair accepts a proton, making an ammonium salt that dissolves readily in water.

Example: many amine drugs are sold as their hydrochloride salts so that they dissolve in water.
cards.searchQuery: amine reacts with HCl ammonium salt methylammonium chloride

cards.title: A ketone is reduced with sodium borohydride, $\ce{NaBH4}$. What class of compound forms?
cards.body:
A secondary alcohol

The carbonyl carbon gains an H and the oxygen becomes an $\ce{-OH}$.

Example: propanone, $\ce{CH3COCH3}$, is reduced to propan-2-ol.

Key idea: ketone gives secondary alcohol; aldehyde gives primary alcohol. Oxidation goes the other way.
cards.searchQuery: reduction of ketone with sodium borohydride gives secondary alcohol

cards.title: An aldehyde is reduced with sodium borohydride, $\ce{NaBH4}$. What class of compound forms?
cards.body:
A primary alcohol

Example: ethanal, $\ce{CH3CHO}$, is reduced to ethanol, $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$.

Watch out: **reduction** here adds hydrogen to the carbonyl, which is the reverse of oxidizing the alcohol.
cards.searchQuery: reduction of aldehyde with sodium borohydride gives primary alcohol

cards.title: Which test uses $\ce{[Ag(NH3)2]+}$ and gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones?
cards.body:
Tollens' test

The aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylate, while $\ce{Ag+}$ is reduced to metallic silver, which coats the glass as a mirror.

Why: ketones have no H on the carbonyl carbon, so they are not oxidized under these mild conditions.
cards.searchQuery: Tollens test silver mirror aldehyde versus ketone

cards.title: Why does benzene typically undergo substitution reactions rather than addition reactions?
cards.body:
Substitution keeps the stable delocalized $\pi$ system; addition would destroy it.

Benzene's aromatic stabilization makes it much less reactive than an ordinary alkene. When it does react, it keeps the ring and swaps an H for another group.

Example: bromine does not decolorize with benzene alone. With an $\ce{FeBr3}$ catalyst it gives bromobenzene and $\ce{HBr}$.
cards.searchQuery: benzene substitution instead of addition aromatic stability delocalized

cards.title: Bromoethane is warmed with aqueous $\ce{NaOH}$. What is the main organic product?
cards.body:
Ethanol

$$\ce{CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + Br-}$$

The hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile and replaces the bromine, a **nucleophilic substitution**.

Watch out: in ethanolic (not aqueous) hot $\ce{KOH}$, the same halide mainly undergoes elimination instead.
cards.searchQuery: bromoethane aqueous NaOH nucleophilic substitution ethanol

cards.title: Bromoethane is heated with $\ce{KOH}$ dissolved in ethanol. What is the main organic product?
cards.body:
Ethene

$$\ce{CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH2=CH2 + H2O + Br-}$$

The hydroxide ion acts as a base and removes an H from the neighboring carbon while the bromide leaves, an **elimination** reaction.

Key idea: aqueous $\ce{OH-}$ favors substitution; hot ethanolic $\ce{OH-}$ favors elimination.
cards.searchQuery: bromoethane ethanolic KOH elimination ethene alkene

cards.title: Which reacts fastest in nucleophilic substitution: $\ce{CH3CH2Cl}$, $\ce{CH3CH2Br}$ or $\ce{CH3CH2I}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{CH3CH2I}$ (iodoethane)

The $\ce{C-I}$ bond is the longest and weakest of the three, and $\ce{I-}$ is the best leaving group.

Key idea: the reactivity order is $\ce{R-I} > \ce{R-Br} > \ce{R-Cl}$, set by the **carbon–halogen bond strength**, not the electronegativity.
cards.searchQuery: haloalkane reactivity iodo bromo chloro C-X bond strength leaving group

cards.title: What functional group links amino acids together in a protein?
cards.body:
Amide (the peptide bond)

The $\ce{-COOH}$ of one amino acid and the $\ce{-NH2}$ of the next join with the loss of water: $\ce{-CO-NH-}$.

Why: the C–N bond has partial double-bond character, so the peptide group is planar and does not rotate freely.
cards.searchQuery: peptide bond amide functional group amino acids protein

cards.title: Which two functional groups are on the central carbon of every amino acid, besides its side chain?
cards.body:
An amino group, $\ce{-NH2}$, and a carboxyl group, $\ce{-COOH}$.

The central ($\alpha$) carbon also carries an H and the side chain R. In water at neutral pH, the molecule exists as a **zwitterion**, $\ce{-NH3+}$ and $\ce{-COO-}$.

Key idea: an amino acid is both an amine (base) and a carboxylic acid.
cards.searchQuery: amino acid structure amino group carboxyl group alpha carbon zwitterion

cards.title: What functional group links the fatty acids to glycerol in a triglyceride (fat)?
cards.body:
Ester

Glycerol has three $\ce{-OH}$ groups, and each one forms an ester bond with the $\ce{-COOH}$ of a fatty acid, releasing three water molecules.

Example: heating a fat with aqueous NaOH breaks the three ester bonds, which is how soap is made.
cards.searchQuery: triglyceride ester linkage glycerol fatty acids structure

cards.title: Why are saturated fats usually solid at room temperature while unsaturated oils are usually liquid?
cards.body:
Cis double bonds put kinks in the fatty acid chains, so unsaturated chains pack poorly and have weaker dispersion forces.

Straight saturated chains stack closely, with more contact between neighboring chains, so more energy is needed to melt them.

Example: butter and lard are rich in saturated fat; olive oil is mostly unsaturated.
cards.searchQuery: saturated versus unsaturated fats melting point cis double bond kinks packing

cards.title: A strong, sharp infrared absorption near $1700\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ indicates which bond or group?
cards.body:
The carbonyl group, $\ce{C=O}$

It appears in aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and amides, usually between about $1650$ and $1800\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

Tip: a strong peak near $1700$ is the quickest sign of a **carbonyl** in an unknown compound.
cards.searchQuery: infrared spectroscopy carbonyl C=O stretch 1700 cm-1

cards.title: A broad, strong infrared absorption at $3200$–$3600\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ is typical of which bond?
cards.body:
O–H (as in an alcohol)

The peak is broad because of hydrogen bonding between molecules. In a carboxylic acid, the O–H absorption is even broader and lower, about $2500$–$3300\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

Watch out: an N–H stretch also appears near $3300\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, but it is sharper and weaker.
cards.searchQuery: infrared spectroscopy O-H stretch broad 3300 cm-1 alcohol
